subject: armadillo
reasoning:
I'm planning the armadillo's proportions and skeleton structure, laying out a root joint, spine chain, neck, head, jaw, tail, legs, and ears to build a believable rig efficiently.

Now I'm working out the body shell geometry—lofting ellipse-shaped sections along the spine to form the domed shell, with countershading paint for dark-backed, pinkish-bellied coloring and banded stripe patterns across the shell plates.

For the armor detail, I'm planning raised band ridges around the body using thin sweep loops positioned on an upper arc of each body section, computed from the body's width and height functions at each z-station.

Defining body stations...

Still designing ridge geometry...

For shields I'm planning to apply different paint patterns based on z-position—stripes in the band zones and scales elsewhere—then settling on an armadillo-appropriate palette: tan-gray shell, darker scale edges, and a pinkish-tan belly tone.

Now I'm designing the head as a tapering loft from skull to snout tip with a dedicated head joint, sizing each station down toward the nose. I'm adding a small dark pink nose sphere, a separate lower jaw loft on its own joint, tiny black eye spheres, and starting on upright ear geometry.

Flattened ear spheres tilted outward at the top sides of the head, with small pink inner-ear details, now move into leg construction -- each leg built as a hip-knee-ankle-toe joint chain swept with a tapered radius, plus a box foot part at the ankle.

Now I'm adding claw spikes to the front feet, tapered and angled downward-forward with a light cream color, weighted to the nearest joint. For the legs themselves I'm mirroring left and right using a sign loop, defining hind leg joint chains from hip through knee, ankle, and toe with feet extending forward along the ground plane.

Still writing leg chains...

Now I'm shaping the tail with a catmull path tapering from thick at the rump to thin at the tip, with scale-pattern stripes layered along it, making sure it stays clear of the floor and roots properly inside the body. Then I'm building the spine chain as a root joint plus three spans running from the rump through the body.

For the head, I'm attaching it to the spine chain's end joint with the jaw parented to the head, routing the tail off the root and splitting leg parenting so hind legs attach near the rump and front legs attach further up the spine. The body loft uses the spine chain as its skinning bone across all three spans, and I'm defining head loft stations tapering width and height as the head extends and lifts forward.

I'm placing the jaw as its own small loft under the head with its own joint for articulation, then adding the nose, eyes, and ears as discrete parts attached to the head bone, with ear joints pointing upward so they can later be posed, plus inner-ear detail spheres offset forward for depth. I'm also setting up a shell paint pattern on the head top to give it a scaled look contrasting with the plain skin below.

For the body, I'm defining a scale-texture paint and a darker banded stripe paint, blending them by z-position across the shell, then applying a countershade so the belly reads lighter than the back using a soft transition blend with a mottled skin tone underneath.

Now I'm placing ridge stations along the back at regular z-intervals, interpolating width and height at each point to build small protruding elliptical ridges with a muted brown color, swept along a smooth catmull path for a continuous raised spine effect.

For the limbs, I'm defining leg and arm chains for each side, placing joint points from shoulder to hand and hip to toe with tapering sweep radii so the limbs narrow toward the paws, keeping foot tips resting at ground level. I'm also setting up small claw loops offset slightly outward at the toe tips to give each foot a few clawed points.

For the tail, I'm using a catmull chain of five points curving down and back from the body, tapering in radius from thick at the base to thin at the tip, and tuning the lengths and heights so it stays short and drags near the ground without floating. I'm giving the tail its own scale-pattern paint with alternating dark bands to distinguish it visually before finalizing all the proportions and writing out the full model.
